newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria should end price controls, analysts say.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria should end price controls, analysts say.

text.p: Removing administrative controls on trade and prices to liberalise the economy could haul Bulgaria out of its devastating financial crisis, analysts said on Thursday.
Delayed reform and economic mismanagement have thrown Bulgaria's economy into chaos, while 30 days of widespread strikes and political squabbling have further paralysed activity.

After a month-long anti-government campaign by the opposition and street protests fuelled by economic hardship President Petar Stoyanov on Tuesday mediated an agreement for general elections by April 20.

"The new political rulers will be much more liberal and transition to a market economy must be done in a fast-forward mode to compensate the delay of the past seven years," said Ivan Krastev, co-director of the independent Institute for Liberal Strategies think-tank.
With January inflation expected at more than 50 percent, hyper-inflation has become a factor for the first time. Shops are closing as the impoverished population concentrate on securing basic foods.
The lev collapsed to 2,800 to the dollar on Thursday from 600 at the beginning of the year and the central bank has exhausted its arsenal of monetary instruments to support the lev.

"The only thing that can be done now is to lift price controls and remove administrative trade restrictions in foreign currency," said Krassen Stanchev, director of the independent Institute for Market Economics.
Despite a ban on trade in foreign currency inside Bulgaria, many restaurants, shops and wholesale suppliers prefer payment in dollars.

"When the conditions for doing business in the country become the same as those outside it, then the people who earn dollars abroad will invest them in Bulgaria, rather than deposit them abroad," said Stanchev.
Current price controls on electricity rates, rail tickets and other goods and services can no longer be adjusted to the lev's volatility and will only fuel deficits, he said.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) proposed the implementation of a currency board last year to halt the freefall of the national currency and to restore confidence in ailing local banks.
The system requires levs in circulation to be matched by central bank reserves, severely curbing the financial powers of the government and the central bank.
The Fund is prepared to resume talks on the implementation of the currency board as soon as there was a government in place. Stoyanov is expected to appoint a caretaker government by February 19.
Radical structural reform, including closing loss-making enterprises and banks, is also part of the reform package.
"Resolving the political crisis will not stop people who can no longer afford food from looting shops," Krastev told Reuters, referring to media reports of attacks on food shops in the countryside.
Long queues often form outside bread shops as people try to stockpile food before prices go up the next day.
Reform laggard Bulgaria is readier than ever for radical measures as a result of the crisis, said Krastev.

The currency board now has more chances of stabilising Bulgaria's economy as it will be introduced after hyper-inflation has eroded domestic debt of more than one trillion levs ($363 million), which was a serious obstruction, said Krastev.

"People will support the currency board because now they know it will save them from hyper-inflation and from complete distortion of their lifestyle. It will give them the chance to plan their lives and businesses," said Krastev.
